lesson.title: Domain and Range
lesson.summary: Every function has a set of allowed inputs and a resulting set of outputs; this section explains what limits these sets and how to find them.
lesson.body:
You already know that a function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input. That word "each" hides an important question: each input from *where*? A function doesn't have to accept every conceivable number ,  it only makes sense on some collection of inputs, and that collection is called the domain. Once you feed every allowed input through the rule, the collection of values that come out the other side is called the range. Domain lives on the input side, range lives on the output side, and neither one is optional information ,  they're part of what the function actually is.

The domain is often restricted for a very concrete reason: some operations inside the rule simply refuse to produce a real number for certain inputs. Division by zero is undefined, so if a function involves dividing by an expression, any input that makes that expression zero must be excluded. Square roots (and other even roots) are undefined for negative numbers within the real numbers, so if a function involves such a root, only inputs that keep the expression under the root nonnegative are allowed. These aren't arbitrary rules imposed by textbooks ,  they're consequences of what the arithmetic operations can actually do. If you write down a function and never check for these trouble spots, you risk claiming the function works where it silently breaks.

Take f(x) = 1/(x − 3). For any input x, this rule tells you to subtract 3, then divide 1 by the result. That works fine for x = 5 (giving 1/2) or x = 0 (giving −1/3), but at x = 3 the denominator becomes 0, and division by zero has no value. So the domain is every real number except 3. Now consider g(x) = √(x − 4). Here you need x − 4 ≥ 0, meaning x ≥ 4, because the square root of a negative number isn't a real number. The domain of g is all real numbers greater than or equal to 4 ,  nothing smaller is allowed in.

Finding the range usually takes more thought, because you have to reason about what values the output can actually reach, not just what's forbidden. For g(x) = √(x − 4), the smallest input you're allowed to use is x = 4, which gives g(4) = √0 = 0. As x increases beyond 4, x − 4 grows without bound, and so does its square root ,  there's no ceiling. So the range is all real numbers greater than or equal to 0: the function never outputs a negative number, because a square root (as ordinarily defined) never does. Notice how the domain restriction (x ≥ 4) directly produces the range restriction (output ≥ 0) ,  the two are linked through the mechanism of the rule itself, not chosen independently.

A useful habit is to picture the function as a machine and ask two separate questions: which raw materials can I legally put in, and which finished products can actually come out? For f(x) = 1/(x − 3), the range turns out to be every real number except 0, since 1 divided by any nonzero number can get arbitrarily large, arbitrarily close to zero, or negative, but can never equal exactly 0 ,  no input makes 1 divided by something equal 0. Keeping domain and range as separate, purposeful questions ,  rather than one vague notion of "what the function is about" ,  is what will let you later read graphs, compose functions, and check whether an inverse exists, all of which depend on knowing precisely where a function is defined and what it can produce.
